paragraphs: A prediction is easier to trust when the model has encountered relevant examples during training. Gaussian processes naturally connect uncertainty to proximity to observed data, but deep neural networks often lack this behavior. This paper introduces Distance Aware Bottleneck, or DAB, to give neural networks an explicit way to assess how closely a new input relates to their training experience.

DAB builds on information bottleneck methods by learning a codebook: a compressed representation of the inputs encountered during training. For a new example, its distance from that codebook serves as an uncertainty estimate. The codebook therefore connects uncertainty to a learned summary of the training data, while allowing the estimate to be computed deterministically in a single forward pass.

The authors report better detection of out-of-distribution inputs and better prediction of classification mistakes than the compared methods, including ensembles, deep kernel Gaussian processes, and standard information bottleneck approaches. These findings support the usefulness of compressed training-data representations for uncertainty estimation, alongside the practical benefit of obtaining that estimate without repeated model evaluations.
icml-2024-a-rate-distortion-view-of-unce.tldr: Distance Aware Bottleneck estimates uncertainty from a learned training-data codebook, improving reported error and out-of-distribution detection with one forward pass.

paragraphs: Robustness certification for image segmentation asks whether pixel labels remain protected against adversarial changes within a specified range and under stated conditions. When certification uses only fine-grained classes, uncertainty between similar categories can force the method to abstain. This paper explores how a hierarchy of categories can preserve useful certified information in those cases.

The proposed algorithm adaptively moves to a broader category when a more specific label is unstable. This allows a pixel to receive a semantically meaningful guarantee even when its finest classification cannot be certified. The authors formulate this hierarchical setting mathematically and prove the correctness of the algorithm’s guarantees. The tradeoff is explicit: broader labels retain less information.

To evaluate that tradeoff, the paper introduces Certified Information Gain, which accounts for class granularity instead of treating all certified labels as equally informative. Experiments on Cityscapes, PASCAL-Context, ACDC, and COCO-Stuff report higher information gain and fewer abstentions than the compared state-of-the-art method. The results support adapting the specificity of a guarantee to the model’s stability.
icml-2024-adaptive-hierarchical-certific.tldr: Adaptive hierarchical certification reduces abstentions by certifying broader pixel categories when fine-grained labels are unstable, while accounting for lost specificity.

paragraphs: A variational quantum eigensolver has an objective with enough structure to support sequential minimal optimization, which needs only a few observations per iteration. Those observations can still be expensive: quantum measurement noise means that evaluating one point typically requires averaging hundreds to thousands of measurement shots. The paper addresses the measurement cost hidden inside each optimization step.

Its method, Subspace in Confident Region, or SubsCoRe, uses a Gaussian process surrogate to represent the objective and its uncertainty. Before optimizing the subspace selected for an update, the method requires sufficiently low uncertainty throughout that subspace. This requirement connects the reliability of each optimization step to the quality of the observations supporting it.

SubsCoRe adapts the required accuracy as optimization progresses, then identifies the minimum number of measurement shots and their distribution that satisfy its confidence requirement. The central contribution is thus a way to allocate measurement effort according to the current optimization need. The stated accuracy guarantee applies through the subspace uncertainty requirement, making precision and observation cost parts of the same decision.
icml-2024-adaptive-observation-cost-cont.tldr: SubsCoRe adapts quantum measurement effort to the surrogate uncertainty and accuracy required for each optimization step.

paragraphs: Regression models predict numerical values, but a prediction alone does not indicate whether its error is likely to be unacceptable. Unreliability can arise from variability inherent in the data or from deficiencies in the model. This paper makes the target explicit by defining an unreliable regression outcome as one whose discrepancy exceeds a specified error threshold.

The method uses probabilistic modeling to estimate the distribution of prediction discrepancies. It then assesses the statistical diversity of that distribution with a proposed measure of statistical dissimilarity. These ingredients produce a data-driven uncertainty score for a regression outcome. The approach therefore uses information about possible errors to assess reliability, with the chosen discrepancy threshold defining what counts as a problematic prediction.

Across multiple regression tasks, the authors report improved error detection and consistent advantages over popular baseline approaches. The practical meaning is that the score can help identify predictions that warrant less confidence. The reported contribution concerns recognizing unreliable outcomes; its empirical support comes from better detection of errors across the evaluated tasks.
icml-2024-beyond-the-norms-detecting-pre.tldr: The paper models prediction discrepancies to build an uncertainty score that improves detection of unreliable regression outputs in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Federated learning can be manipulated by adversarial clients that submit arbitrary updates. A common defense replaces the server’s ordinary average with a robust averaging rule, producing the method studied here as FedRo. The paper examines how this defense interacts with two routine choices: sampling only some clients and allowing clients to take multiple local optimization steps.

These choices create distinct difficulties. Subsampling increases the effective fraction of adversarial clients, while local steps increase disagreement among honest clients’ updates. For smooth non-convex losses, the authors derive a sufficient subsampling condition for nearly optimal convergence. They also identify a threshold beyond which sampling additional clients brings diminishing improvements in learning accuracy.

Local computation has a more favorable effect under carefully chosen step sizes: the learning error attributable to adversarial clients decreases as the number of local steps grows. Experiments on FEMNIST and CIFAR-10 support the theory. The results show why robust averaging must be analyzed together with participation and update schedules, and why the benefits of additional clients or local steps depend on how those choices are configured.
icml-2024-byzantine-robust-federated-lea.tldr: The paper characterizes how client sampling and local updates affect robust federated learning, including conditions for convergence and reduced adversarial error.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised learning can spread label information from annotated examples to unlabeled data using relationships among samples. Ordinary graphs represent pairwise relationships, while hypergraphs can directly represent connections involving whole groups. This richer representation is useful for relationships such as group membership, but the nonlinear hypergraph Laplacian has made large-scale computation difficult.

The paper develops scalable algorithms for core hypergraph computations, including PageRank vectors and Laplacian systems. These operations provide the computational machinery needed to diffuse information through hypergraph models. The algorithms apply to general families of hypergraphs and come with theoretical guarantees, addressing a bottleneck that previously restricted the practical use of these richer structures.

The authors demonstrate speed on semi-supervised learning benchmarks involving categorical data. They also use the algorithms’ generality to improve semi-supervised manifold clustering with hypergraph models. The stated significance is both computational and representational: speeding up fundamental operations makes it more practical to use group relationships in learning problems at massive scale.
icml-2024-fast-algorithms-for-hypergraph.tldr: Fast hypergraph PageRank and Laplacian algorithms make higher-order relationships more practical for large-scale semi-supervised learning.

paragraphs: Semidefinite programming can express large optimization problems, but solving them efficiently remains difficult. Matrix sketching has helped existing solvers handle larger problems, at the expense of more iterations as size grows. Their iteration-dependent parameter schedules also hinder warm starts, where a useful initial solution is available from related work or previously received data.

The paper introduces Unified Spectral Bundling with Sketching, or USBS, a provably correct spectral bundle algorithm for problems containing equality and inequality constraints. An optional matrix sketch reduces the representation burden while sustaining convergence speed. The algorithm can also exploit a warm-start initialization, making previously obtained solutions useful for accelerating subsequent optimization.

Experiments across several applications demonstrate the method with and without warm starts. One reported instance, involving more than two billion decision variables, shows a 500-fold speedup over the compared state-of-the-art scalable solver. That figure describes a particular instance. More broadly, the contribution combines scalability, convergence speed, and useful initialization within one solver, with a publicly available implementation in JAX.
icml-2024-fast-scalable-warm-start-semid.tldr: USBS combines spectral bundling, optional matrix sketching, and warm starts to solve massive semidefinite programs efficiently.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks may contain more trainable parameters than there are training examples. Understanding their performance on unseen graphs in this over-parameterized setting is difficult, and the paper identifies previous generalization bounds as uninformative there. Its goal is to provide a theoretical framework that yields useful guarantees despite the large number of parameters.

The analysis covers graph convolutional networks and message passing graph neural networks. It studies these architectures in the mean-field regime and derives upper bounds on their generalization error. The reported bounds have a convergence rate of O(1/n), where n counts graph samples. The sample unit matters: the stated rate is expressed in terms of the number of graphs.

This rate describes how the theoretical upper bounds improve as the sample count grows within the analyzed regime. It does not specify the exact error of every trained network. The contribution is a more informative theoretical account of generalization for these two widely used graph architectures when parameter counts exceed the amount of available training data.
icml-2024-generalization-error-of-graph-.tldr: The paper derives O(1/n) generalization-error bounds for two graph neural network families in the over-parameterized mean-field regime.

paragraphs: Optimization algorithms generate a sequence of changes to a model’s parameters. A dynamical-systems perspective studies the behavior of those changes over time, especially what happens as optimization continues. This paper takes that perspective on an extensively studied optimizer, redefining it through classical techniques from hyperbolic geometry.

The authors connect the resulting definition to a nonlinear differential equation through a continuous limit. This connection provides a mathematical description of the optimizer’s evolution in continuous time. Its role is to make the long-term behavior accessible to tools from differential equations and stability analysis, linking the geometric reformulation of the optimizer to a dynamical model.

The paper then uses Lyapunov stability concepts to analyze the asymptotic behavior of critical points. Such analysis concerns how the dynamics behave around those points over time. The stated contribution is a theoretical treatment of the redefined optimizer: hyperbolic geometry supplies its formulation, the continuous limit supplies the differential equation, and stability theory supplies a way to examine its eventual behavior.
icml-2024-hyperbolic-optimizer-as-a-dyna.tldr: The paper reformulates an optimizer using hyperbolic geometry and studies its continuous-time critical-point behavior through Lyapunov stability.

paragraphs: Neural scaling laws describe how model performance changes with training resources and help determine how to allocate a fixed compute budget. Conventional compute-optimal training chooses a model configuration suited to that budget. This paper expands the optimization problem by allowing the model’s shape to change while training is underway.

With an adaptive model, the training process can move between the scaling relationships associated with different shapes. The authors use this freedom to design a path that allocates computation more effectively over the course of training. The key decision therefore includes how model shape evolves, alongside the overall resources invested in reaching a target level of performance.

The paper reports that adaptive models can outpace static counterparts and substantially reduce the computation needed to reach a given target. It also shows that the approach generalizes across modalities and different shape parameters. These findings make the training trajectory itself part of compute optimality: changing the model during learning can improve the efficiency of the overall process.
icml-2024-navigating-scaling-laws-comput.tldr: Allowing model shape to change during training can reduce the computation needed to reach a target performance compared with static models.

paragraphs: A classification coreset is a small subset of data that supports optimization while preserving an approximation guarantee for the original dataset’s loss. Its usefulness depends on how small that subset can be without losing the guarantee. This paper refines sensitivity sampling analysis to obtain coreset sizes that do not depend on the input dimension.

The central technical tool is a version of the sensitivity sampling framework based on Rademacher complexity. This changes the analysis used to establish the approximation guarantees and supports results across a variety of loss functions. The dimensional independence concerns the required coreset size, making the result relevant when each example has many features.

The framework also handles distributional inputs and can use independent, identically distributed samples. That extends the results beyond compressing a fixed dataset and yields sample-complexity bounds. The contribution is therefore both a classification result and an analytical tool: it establishes dimension-independent coresets while developing a sensitivity sampling approach that the authors identify as potentially useful on its own.
icml-2024-no-dimensional-sampling-corese.tldr: A Rademacher-complexity analysis yields classification coresets whose size is independent of input dimension, with extensions to distributional sampling.

paragraphs: Different layers of a normalized neural network can experience very different effective learning rates, even during the same training run. Large disparities can make training difficult. This paper models the evolution of expected gradient norms and weight norms to explain how those layerwise differences change over time.

Within this analysis, the authors prove that effective-learning-rate ratios converge to one under any constant learning rate, even when gradients initially explode. They also identify a critical learning rate, determined only by current effective learning rates, above which disparities widen. These statements describe different aspects of the dynamics: eventual equalization can coexist with an initial period in which differences become larger.

The authors turn the analysis into a warm-up method that requires no hyperparameters and quickly reduces the spread of effective learning rates in theory and practice. Experiments connect that spread to trainability, with the relationship clearest in very deep networks experiencing large changes in gradient magnitude. The work thus provides both an account of layer imbalance and a practical way to reduce it early in training.
icml-2024-on-the-weight-dynamics-of-deep.tldr: The paper explains layerwise effective-learning-rate dynamics and derives a hyperparameter-free warm-up that rapidly reduces their disparities.

paragraphs: Online conformal prediction updates uncertainty estimates as observations arrive. One important goal is coverage: how often the prediction set contains the eventual outcome. Existing methods can provide a retrospective guarantee over an arbitrary observed sequence, but a sequence-level guarantee does not by itself describe coverage at each individual time point.

This paper introduces an online method with decaying step sizes. It preserves the retrospective coverage guarantee for arbitrary sequences while also allowing estimation of a population quantile when that quantile exists. These are complementary properties: the first concerns performance across an observed sequence, while the second concerns learning a stable distributional quantity when one is available.

The theory and experiments indicate substantially improved practical behavior under a stable distribution. In that setting, coverage stays close to the desired level at every time point, rather than only when averaged across the sequence. The distinction matters for interpreting uncertainty as predictions arrive. The stable-distribution result is conditional, while the retrospective guarantee retains its applicability to arbitrary sequences.
icml-2024-online-conformal-prediction-wi.tldr: Decaying step sizes preserve retrospective online coverage while supporting quantile estimation and improved timewise coverage under stable distributions.

paragraphs: A language model may encounter a fact during training yet fail to retrieve it when asked a question. Using a controlled biography dataset, this paper studies the distinction between storing knowledge and making it accessible through question answering. It asks how training-text diversity affects extraction from factual sources, beyond exposure to similar questions.

The experiments find a strong relationship between knowledge extraction and diversity in pretraining data. Augmentations such as paraphrasing and sentence shuffling are needed for reliable extraction in the studied setting. Without such augmentation, knowledge may be memorized yet yield zero question-answering accuracy, even after instruction fine-tuning. This makes the form of exposure during pretraining central to the reported result.

Nearly linear probes connect these outcomes to where knowledge is represented internally: in entity-name embeddings or distributed across other text tokens. The authors recommend rewriting pretraining material with auxiliary models and including more instruction-fine-tuning data during pretraining. These recommendations follow from the controlled finding that later instruction tuning may fail to make already memorized knowledge retrievable.
icml-2024-physics-of-language-models-par.tldr: Controlled biography experiments show that pretraining diversity strongly affects whether memorized facts can later be extracted through question answering.

paragraphs: Researchers sometimes interpret meaningful patterns inside language models as signs of human-like understanding or artificial general intelligence. This position paper challenges that inference. Its central concern is whether correlations between internal representations and external variables provide evidence strong enough to support claims about general intelligence.

The authors probe models spanning random projections, matrix decompositions, deep autoencoders, and transformers. All can retain information useful for predicting latent or external variables. This comparison shows that the presence of predictive information is shared by methods of widely differing complexity. The paper argues, with empirical support, that finding meaningful latent-space patterns cannot itself serve as evidence for AGI.

The authors also draw on social-science research about pattern seeking and anthropomorphism. They argue that these tendencies, together with common experimental setups and AI’s public image, encourage researchers and audiences to attribute observed correlations to understanding. Their recommendation is greater methodological care and academic integrity when interpreting and communicating results, especially when moving from a representation-level observation to a claim about intelligence.
icml-2024-position-stop-making-unscienti.tldr: The paper argues that meaningful patterns in model representations do not establish AGI and calls for more careful interpretation of such evidence.

paragraphs: A dose-response curve describes how a drug’s concentration relates to its inhibition of cell growth. The paper argues that the commonly used Hill-equation model oversimplifies the behavior of many drugs. In those cases, reducing performance to the half-inhibitory concentration, IC50, can mislead treatment recommendations and the selection of promising candidates.

The proposed neural model predicts the entire curve using an embedding of the interaction between a drug molecule and the tissue transcriptome. This representation ties predictions to both the compound and the tissue’s gene-expression information. Predicting the full concentration-response relationship preserves variation that a single summary value cannot describe.

Compared with prior state-of-the-art methods, the model performs better at estimating inhibitory effects for untried concentrations, both within and beyond observed concentration ranges. The authors also report accurate curve predictions for drugs on previously unseen tumor tissues and for previously untested molecules on established tumor cell lines. These findings support learning richer response patterns across the evaluated drug and tissue settings.
icml-2024-predicting-dose-response-curve.tldr: A neural model predicts full drug dose-response curves from drug–tissue interactions, improving reported predictions for new concentrations, tissues, and molecules.

paragraphs: Gaussian process regression commonly assumes independent, identically distributed Gaussian observation noise. That assumption enables convenient closed-form conditioning, but violations can undermine predictions and uncertainty estimates. Existing robust alternatives often lose the closed-form updates, making them more computationally expensive and less convenient to use.

The paper introduces robust and conjugate Gaussian process regression, or RCGP, through generalized Bayesian inference. It provides a provably robust approach while retaining exact, closed-form conjugate updates in every setting where ordinary Gaussian processes admit them. Preserving those updates matters because it keeps the analytical convenience that makes standard Gaussian process regression attractive.

The authors describe the additional computational cost as virtually negligible and demonstrate strong empirical performance in applications ranging from Bayesian optimization to sparse variational Gaussian processes. The main contribution is the combination of robustness and tractable conditioning within the same method. This gives practitioners a way to address the weaknesses of the usual noise assumption while retaining the update structure available in standard GP settings.
icml-2024-robust-and-conjugate-gaussian-.tldr: RCGP uses generalized Bayesian inference to provide provable robustness while preserving standard Gaussian processes’ closed-form updates at virtually no extra cost.

paragraphs: Matching correlated graphs means determining which nodes correspond across two related networks. Corrupted nodes can obscure those correspondences by changing their connections. This paper introduces two corruption models to distinguish the effects of random disruption from those of adversarial manipulation, and studies what matching procedures can recover in each.

In the weak model, a random subset of nodes in one or both graphs interacts randomly with the network. No estimator can correctly recover a positive fraction of the corrupted nodes. For the uncorrupted nodes, the authors derive necessary conditions for complete identification and matching, then show that the k-core estimator succeeds under those same conditions.

In the strong model, an adversary chooses the affected nodes and can alter their interactions arbitrarily. Detecting corrupted nodes is impossible in this model. Nevertheless, when only one network is compromised and appropriate conditions hold, the maximum overlap estimator can correctly match a positive fraction of nodes without explicitly identifying them. The results separate the possibility of recovering correspondences from the possibility of recognizing corruption.
icml-2024-robust-graph-matching-when-nod.tldr: The paper establishes recovery limits and conditional matching guarantees for correlated graphs with random or adversarial node corruption.

paragraphs: Learning a causal graph requires searching among many possible relationships between variables. Conditional-independence tests can narrow that search, but deciding whether two variables are directly connected may require exponentially many tests. This paper targets that adjacency decision as a central obstacle to scaling causal discovery.

The Differentiable Adjacency Test, or DAT, replaces the exponential collection of tests with a relaxed problem that the authors prove equivalent. It solves the resulting problem by training two neural networks. The paper then builds DAT-Graph around this test, creating a graph-learning method that can also incorporate data collected under interventions.

The authors report learning graphs with 1,000 variables at state-of-the-art accuracy. They also use the learned graph to construct models that predict intervention effects much more accurately on large-scale RNA sequencing data. These findings connect the computational reformulation to both graph recovery and downstream intervention prediction. The equivalence result concerns the relaxed adjacency problem, while the reported accuracy demonstrates the practical performance of the complete learning method.
icml-2024-scalable-and-flexible-causal-d.tldr: DAT reformulates adjacency testing as a neural optimization problem, enabling scalable causal graph learning and improved reported intervention predictions.

paragraphs: Exploration is difficult in reinforcement learning when high-dimensional environments require function approximation. The paper proposes studying exploration through policy objectives designed to support later maximization of any reward function. Its new objective, L1-Coverage, provides a common framework for several previous exploration schemes.

The objective is associated with L1-Coverability, a structural quantity that captures intrinsic statistical difficulty in the underlying Markov decision process. The framework encompasses Block and Low-Rank MDPs. When the environment model is known, optimizing coverage efficiently reduces to standard policy optimization, allowing the use of established tools such as policy gradients and Q-learning.

For MDPs with low coverability, the authors obtain computationally efficient model-based and model-free online learning algorithms, covering both reward-free and reward-driven exploration. Experiments also find that L1-Coverage encourages existing policy optimization methods to explore the state space effectively. The contribution links an exploration objective, a structural measure of problem difficulty, and usable optimization machinery, with the efficiency results tied to the stated coverability condition.
icml-2024-scalable-online-exploration-vi.tldr: L1-Coverage connects exploration to standard policy optimization and enables efficient online reinforcement learning in environments with low coverability.

paragraphs: Gaussian process regression depends strongly on its covariance function. Stationary choices are popular, but ordinary non-periodic stationary covariance functions bring mean reversion: predictions tend back toward a fixed global mean. That behavior can be inappropriate for data whose values do not settle toward such a mean.

The paper constructs stationary processes without mean reversion by using improper Gaussian process priors with infinite variance. This limiting setting permits non-positive kernels that are unavailable in the ordinary formulation. Despite the unusual prior, posterior distributions remain analytically computable through a simple correction to the standard formulas.

The authors introduce a broad family of smooth, non-reverting covariance functions resembling familiar squared-exponential and Matérn kernels. Analyses of synthetic and real data show that these kernels resolve some known problems caused by mean reversion while preserving most favorable properties of ordinary smooth stationary kernels. The contribution expands the modeling choices available when stationarity is desirable but attraction toward a fixed global mean conflicts with the data.
icml-2024-stationarity-without-mean-reve.tldr: Improper infinite-variance Gaussian process priors enable stationary, non-mean-reverting models with analytically computable posteriors.

paragraphs: Decentralized learning keeps data distributed and avoids a central coordinator, but exchanged models can still reveal private information. The paper proposes Decor, a differentially private variant of decentralized stochastic gradient descent. It protects local models by coordinating the noise that users add during communication.

Users first securely exchange randomness seeds, then generate correlated Gaussian noise that cancels pairwise. This noise protects local models at every communication round. The privacy analysis uses SecLDP, a proposed relaxation of local differential privacy that assumes each connected pair of users shares a secret hidden from everyone else. Under that assumption, it protects communications against external eavesdroppers and curious users.

For arbitrary connected communication graphs, the authors theoretically and empirically show that Decor matches the optimal central-DP privacy–utility tradeoff under SecLDP. A central analytical challenge is controlling correlated noise that fails to cancel because the network is sparse. The paper also provides a privacy accountant. The result shows the value of coordinated randomness under the specified secret-sharing assumption and privacy definition.
icml-2024-the-privacy-power-of-correlate.tldr: Decor uses correlated noise to match the central-DP privacy–utility tradeoff under SecLDP, assuming secret sharing between connected users.

paragraphs: Language models can lose coherence and processing ability when inputs exceed the sequence lengths used in pretraining. Extending that range through further training on long sequences can be expensive. This paper introduces Dual Chunk Attention, or DCA, as a way to extend context length without additional training.

DCA decomposes attention for a long sequence into chunk-based components. It handles relative positions both within a chunk and across different chunks, allowing the model to preserve positional information across the longer input. The method also integrates with Flash Attention. Its main mechanism is therefore a change in attention computation that supports extrapolation beyond the original training length.

The authors report that DCA enables Llama2 70B to support contexts of up to 100,000 tokens. On the practical long-context tasks evaluated, performance is comparable to or better than that of models extended through continual training. The findings demonstrate the potential of modifying attention to obtain useful long-context behavior while avoiding the expense of an additional training stage.
icml-2024-training-free-long-context-sca.tldr: Dual Chunk Attention extends Llama2 70B to contexts of up to 100,000 tokens without training by reorganizing attention within and across chunks.

paragraphs: Evaluating code language models often relies on small, manually curated benchmarks that cover a narrow slice of software development. Building comparable evaluations for more domains requires substantial human effort. This paper introduces round-trip correctness as a way to expand evaluation using existing code without costly human annotation.

The method asks a model to transform an input and then uses that prediction to transform back. For example, a model can describe code in natural language and then generate code from the description. Evaluation checks whether the resulting code is semantically equivalent to the original: whether the round trip preserves its meaning or behavior.

The authors apply this idea to code synthesis and editing. They find that round-trip correctness strongly correlates with performance on existing narrow-domain synthesis benchmarks, while enabling evaluation across a much wider collection of domains and tasks. That correlation supports the method’s relevance to established evaluation targets. Its broader contribution is to make evaluation less dependent on separately curated human annotations for every new software setting.
icml-2024-unsupervised-evaluation-of-cod.tldr: Round-trip correctness evaluates code models through semantic reconstruction, broadening task coverage while correlating strongly with established synthesis benchmarks.

paragraphs: Image watermarks can indicate provenance or identify artificially generated content, but their usefulness depends on surviving changes to an image. WAVES is a benchmark for assessing that robustness through a standardized collection of stress tests. It brings watermark detection and identification tasks into a common evaluation protocol.

The tests range from traditional image distortions to new variations of diffusion-based and adversarial attacks. Evaluation considers two dimensions together: how much an attack degrades image quality and how effectively the watermark can still be detected afterward. Considering both helps characterize the relationship between damage to the visible image and damage to its embedded identifying signal.

Using this broader evaluation, the authors uncover previously undetected vulnerabilities in several modern watermarking algorithms. The result demonstrates that a more varied set of stress tests can expose weaknesses missed by existing evaluation methods. WAVES is presented as a toolkit for developing more robust watermarks, providing a shared way to assess how watermark behavior changes across different attacks and image-quality outcomes.
icml-2024-waves-benchmarking-the-robustn.tldr: WAVES standardizes image-watermark stress testing and reveals previously undetected vulnerabilities by evaluating detection alongside image degradation.
